architecture/determinism.title: Determinism — same seed, same inputs, same end state
architecture/determinism.content:
Determinism — same seed, same inputs, same end state
The contract: same start state, same inputs, same seed → same end state, byte for byte. It is what makes the game testable without a window, replayable, and the foundation for rollback netcode and RL training.
What it takes:

Ticks, not seconds (ADR-0003): all durations are integer ticks; TICKS_PER_SECOND only converts per-second balance rates.
One seeded RNG (ADR-0004): SimRng, Xoshiro256** with SplitMix64, seeded from the scenario. No other randomness — enforced by clippy.toml.
No hash maps in the simulation: HashMap/HashSet (std’s, Bevy’s, hashbrown’s) iterate in an order that depends on hashing or insertion history; BTreeMap/BTreeSet instead (enforced by clippy.toml, which also forbids rand and getrandom should they ever become dependencies).
Ordering by SimId (ADR-0008): never by Entity.
Floating point discipline: the same operations in the same order on all platforms; only operations IEEE 754 defines exactly (+ - * /, sqrt), no sin, cos, powf and the like, whose results come from the platform’s maths library; cross-platform floating-point determinism for real PvP is an open question (see the problem log).
No clocks: no Instant::now, no SystemTime::now in the simulation; count ticks.
One tick rate: SimPlugin sets the fixed timestep to TICKS_PER_SECOND (Bevy’s default is 64 Hz; the value 60 is a template default, ADR-0014); systems use TICK_SECONDS, never Time.
One seeding point: scenario::start_run seeds SimRng from the scenario before the game spawns, for the client and the headless app alike; IDs come from the SimIdCounter resource.
Intents in actor order: TickIntents is sorted by SimId, not by arrival.
Complete snapshots: everything that changes during a run is captured by Snapshot (tick, RNG, ID counter, who controls which actor, the game’s state), and the state hash covers all of it, including all four words of the RNG state; tests/snapshot.rs proves it by re-running from a restored snapshot.

How it is tested: Determinism test, and a committed regression replay that every CI platform plays back. What it enables: Network.

architecture/intent-and-controls.title: Intent & controls — the one thing the presentation writes back
architecture/intent-and-controls.content:
Intent & controls — the one thing the presentation writes back
The presentation never touches simulation state. It produces an intent: plain, serialisable data (serde), no Bevy types, no entity handles (ADR-0002). That is what makes intents usable by a player, an AI, an add-on, a replay, and the network alike.
struct Intent { player: PlayerId, actor: SimId, action: Action }   // core: game_sim::intent
enum Action { Move { x: f32, z: f32 }, Idle }      // the game's: game_sim::game (example, ADR-0013)
Rules:

Intents are queued in the IntentBuffer. At the start of each tick (SimSet::Input) they are checked and frozen into TickIntents, sorted by actor (arrival order kept per actor): arrival order differs between machines, SimId order does not. Game systems read TickIntents only.
Checked before any game system sees them: the game’s validate must accept the action, and the Control resource must say the sending player controls the actor. Everything else lands in RejectedIntents with its reason (Security). The game assigns control when it spawns actors and changes it when they change hands.
In the client, the input layer (ADR-0016) turns devices into actions; the presentation turns actions into intents, once per tick, in FixedPreUpdate.
Input is mapped through actions, never raw key codes; keyboard/mouse and gamepad are equal.
Extend Action with the game’s abilities; once variants travel the network, they are stable (see Serialization & IDs).
No visible text in code; everything goes through localisation keys.

architecture/network.title: Network — rollback with the server as referee
architecture/network.content:
Network — rollback with the server as referee
PvP is designed, not built yet. The template default (ADR-0006, decided per game): rollback netcode, with a server as referee. The rollback itself exists headless (game_sim::rollback, tested); transport and server do not.
client A ──intent──▶ ┌─────────┐ ◀──intent── client B
   ▲                  │ server  │              ▲
   └──observation──── │ referee │ ──observation┘

Each client simulates itself — locally, at full frame rate, predicting ahead on its own intent.
On a late intent, the client rewinds to the last confirmed tick, applies it, and re-simulates to the present: rollback. This is only possible because the simulation is deterministic (Determinism) and intents are plain data (Intent & controls).
The server is the referee: it validates intents, keeps the authoritative tick, and decides conflicts. When client and server disagree, the server wins.
Each client sees only what it may see: the server sends the observation with the visibility filter of that team (Observation, Security).

Open questions live in the problem log: transport crate, hit rating under latency, direct client connections.

architecture/observation.title: Observation — the single code path for reading state
architecture/observation.content:
Observation — the single code path for reading state
HUD, AI, add-ons and the network never query the ECS world directly. They all read through the one observation interface: a function that snapshots the simulation state a given team is allowed to see, with a visibility filter (ADR-0007).
Why one code path:

Visibility is a simulation concern: what a team cannot see, it must not receive — one filter, one place to audit.
AI and RL train on exactly what a player sees, no more.
The network sends exactly what the observation returns; no second, leakier path.

In code: game_sim::observation::observe(world, viewer) returns the tick and the game’s GameObservation; the visibility filter is the game’s game::observe (the example shows everything). The client’s presentation reads only this, once per tick, and draws between the last two observations.
Rules: the observation is read-only, returns plain data (serialisable, no Entity), and is versioned like the intent. Whoever touches visibility or the network reads Security first.

architecture/overview.title: Overview — the system in one diagram
architecture/overview.content:
Overview — the system in one diagram
        intents (serialisable data)
  ┌──────────────┐              ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Presentation │  ──intent──▶ │    Simulation      │
  │ game_client  │              │ game_sim, FixedUpdate│
  │ camera, HUD, │ ◀─observation─ deterministic tick │
  │ input, audio │              │ chain, seeded RNG  │
  └──────────────┘              └────────────────────┘
        ▲                                 ▲
        │                        confirmed state / rollback
   player input                        (later: server)
The one big bet: gameplay is a deterministic, headless tick simulation (Simulation model). Everything else follows from it:

The presentation is a pure observer; it writes back exactly one thing, the intent.
Everything that reads state — HUD, AI, add-ons, the network — reads through the observation.
Randomness comes only from the seeded RNG, time only from ticks (Determinism).
Later, PvP runs as rollback netcode with a server as referee, which the determinism makes possible.

Why this architecture: it makes the game testable without a window, replayable, desync-debuggable, and it is the foundation for rollback netcode and RL-trained AI.

architecture/platforms.title: Platforms — targets and what excludes them
architecture/platforms.content:
Platforms — targets and what excludes them
Targets: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS (tier 1: full gates), Web (wasm32) when feasible. The simulation crate must build for wasm32-unknown-unknown (ADR-0009): no threads, no file system, no system time, no clock.

























TierPlatformsCI1Windows, Linux, macOScargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets, cargo test2Android, iOScargo check -p game_sim for the target3Web (wasm32)cargo check -p game_sim --target wasm32-unknown-unknown; cargo build -p game_client --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
The web build of the client only proves that it compiles and links for wasm32-unknown-unknown (a full build, because only linking finds a dependency without a wasm32 implementation). Nothing runs it: no wasm-bindgen step, no page, no browser test. Shipping to the web is a per-game task.
Rules:

Nothing goes in that excludes a platform; every new dependency is checked for platform support before it enters Cargo.toml. Checked so far beyond Bevy and Avian: serde, and postcard (no_std with alloc; builds for every target, ADR-0017); in the client base64 (pure Rust, every target) and, on the web only, web-sys and wasm-bindgen (already in the graph through Bevy).
The simulation never touches a file system: saves and replays are bytes; the client stores them where the platform allows (game_client/src/storage.rs): a file in the user’s data folder on Windows, Linux and macOS, in the app container’s Library/Application Support on iOS and in the app’s internal data folder on Android; the browser’s localStorage on the web. The table is at the top of storage.rs.
The client uses Bevy’s default features (window, renderer, winit); the simulation does not (ADR-0005).
On Android, Bevy links android-activity; the android-check feature of game_sim exists only so CI can check the crate alone.

Input: actions, not key codes — keyboard/mouse and gamepad are equal on every platform.

architecture/security.title: Security — how the server, PvP and add-ons are kept safe
architecture/security.content:
Security — how the server, PvP and add-ons are kept safe
Mandatory reading for every change that touches the network, external input or add-ons.

The client is in the hands of the enemy. Every intent that reaches a server or another client is untrusted input: validate range, rate and ownership before it enters a simulation. The simulation already enforces two of these at the start of every tick (intent::freeze_intents): the game’s validate refuses malformed actions (NaN, infinity, out of range), and Control refuses intents from a player for an actor it does not control. Rejected intents are listed in RejectedIntents with the reason. Rate limits belong to the server. Over the network, the server sets an intent’s player from the connection, never from the message.
The server is the referee (ADR-0006): it validates intents, owns the authoritative tick and decides conflicts. A client never trusts another client’s state, only the server’s observation.
Visibility is enforced by the server (Observation): what a team cannot see, it never receives. A client cannot leak what it never had.
Add-ons produce intents, nothing else (see Extension points): they run sandboxed, read through the observation, and can never touch simulation state, the network or the file system.
No secrets in the client and none in the repository (.env, .secrets are gitignored and never committed).
Determinism is integrity: a desync between client and server is a bug and a cheat detector at once; the determinism test is part of the security posture.

architecture/serialization-and-ids.title: Serialization & IDs — what travels the network
architecture/serialization-and-ids.content:
Serialization & IDs — what travels the network
Two kinds of data ever leave the simulation: intents in, observations out. Both are plain serde data (ADR-0002); Bevy’s Reflect is not used on the wire — enum discriminants and field order stay under our control.
Rules:

Simulation entities are identified by SimId (ADR-0008), a dense i64 assigned in spawn order. Never serialise Entity.
Action variants and observation fields are stable once released: adding is fine, renumbering or changing meaning is a breaking change that needs a version flag.
Serialisation is deterministic: BTreeMap, not HashMap; sorted lists, not iteration order.
Everything the network accepts is untrusted input; see Security.

How this feeds rollback: Network.

architecture/simulation-model.title: Simulation model — the invariants and the tick chain
architecture/simulation-model.content:
Simulation model — the invariants and the tick chain
The entire gameplay is a deterministic tick simulation in FixedUpdate (ADR-0001). One source per fact: the invariants live here, the reasoning in the ADRs.
Invariants

One tick, one chain. Every gameplay system runs in FixedUpdate, in SimSet::Update, in exactly one of the game’s own ordered sets. Nothing gameplay runs anywhere else.
No frame time. The simulation never reads wall-clock or frame deltas; all durations are ticks (ADR-0003).
One randomness source. All randomness draws from SimRng; clippy.toml forbids everything else (ADR-0004).
Ordering by SimId. Never by Entity; entity indices are ephemeral and unordered (ADR-0008).
Presentation is an observer. It writes exactly one thing back: the intent (ADR-0002). The simulation never reads presentation state.
One code path per quantity. Damage, health, death — each has exactly one place where it happens.
No gameplay state in Local<>, no meshes, materials, lights or UI on simulation entities.
Teams, not “the opponent”. No code assumes exactly two players.

The tick chain
The core owns three sets (game_sim::schedule::SimSet), in this order every tick:





















SetWhat happensInputThe tick is counted (SimTick), the queued intents are frozen into TickIntents in actor order, and recorded if a replay is recording.UpdateThe game’s systems, in the game’s own ordered sets.EndEnd-of-tick work of the core (empty so far: checks, statistics).
Inside Update, the example game (ADR-0013, a template default) runs:
Intent  →  Values  →  Movement  →  Damage  →  Cleanup





























SetWhat happensIntentThis tick’s intents set the units’ velocities.ValuesCooldowns, regeneration, attribute modifiers (empty in the example).MovementUnits move by their velocity and are clamped to the arena.DamageHits, effects, damage and death, sorted by SimId (empty in the example).CleanupSpent entities are despawned, respawns happen (empty in the example).
A new game replaces these stages with its own; the order is the contract that keeps runs reproducible.

Pinned natively by web_keys_carry_the_app_and_refuse_bad_slots and text_encoding_round_trips_every_byte.
Checked: web in headless Chromium (wasm-bindgen 0.2.130, debug build): F5 in a run wrote game_client/quicksave; after a page reload, F9 on the menu started the saved run. Desktop unchanged (tests green).

Check on a device or emulator when that packaging exists; then set this task to done.

decisions/adr-0001-tick-simulation-in-fi.title: ADR-0001 — Tick simulation in FixedUpdate instead of frame deltas
decisions/adr-0001-tick-simulation-in-fi.content:
ADR-0001 — Tick simulation in FixedUpdate instead of frame deltas
Status: accepted
Context: The game must be testable without a window, replayable, and later run as rollback netcode and RL training. Frame-dependent simulation is none of that: results depend on the machine, and tests would need a renderer.
Decision: The entire gameplay runs in Bevy’s FixedUpdate as a tick simulation: fixed timestep, one tick = 1 / TICKS_PER_SECOND seconds. Every gameplay system lives in the tick chain (schedule.rs).
Rejected alternative: Simulating with the frame delta in Update. Simpler at first, but results differ per frame rate, replays and rollback become impossible, and tests need a window.
Consequences: Determinism by construction; headless tests, replays and rollback become possible. Costs: animation must interpolate between ticks; designers think in ticks, not seconds.

decisions/adr-0002-intent-as-serialisabl.title: ADR-0002 — Intent as serialisable data instead of raw input
decisions/adr-0002-intent-as-serialisabl.content:
ADR-0002 — Intent as serialisable data instead of raw input
Status: accepted
Context: Input reaches the simulation from more than one source: a local player, an AI, an add-on, a replay file, the network. Raw Res<Input<KeyCode>> in simulation systems would couple the simulation to one device and make all other sources impossible.
Decision: The presentation (or AI, add-on, network) produces an intent: plain, serde-serialisable data — no Bevy types, no entity handles. The simulation consumes intents and nothing else. This is the single thing the presentation writes back.
Rejected alternative: Reading Input<KeyCode> directly in simulation systems. Fewer indirections, but device-bound, not serialisable, not trainable, not networkable.
Consequences: One input model for player, AI, add-on, replay and network; rollback can record and replay intents. Costs: an extra layer between device and simulation; intents need a stable format once they travel the network.

decisions/adr-0003-ticks-instead-of-seco.title: ADR-0003 — Ticks instead of seconds for all timers
decisions/adr-0003-ticks-instead-of-seco.content:
ADR-0003 — Ticks instead of seconds for all timers
Status: accepted
Context: Cooldowns, durations, regeneration — all gameplay timing must survive a rollback (rewind and re-simulate) and produce identical results everywhere. Floating-point seconds accumulate rounding differences per frame and per platform.
Decision: All durations in the simulation are integer ticks. TICKS_PER_SECOND exists only to convert per-second balance rates into per-tick values.
Rejected alternative: f32/f64 seconds with Timer resources. Reads naturally, but accumulates error, is hard to rewind, and desyncs across platforms.
Consequences: Exact, rewindable timing; balance rates need a documented conversion point. Costs: designers and players think in seconds, so balance data carries both.

decisions/adr-0004-one-seeded-rng-resour.title: ADR-0004 — One seeded RNG resource instead of scattered generators
decisions/adr-0004-one-seeded-rng-resour.content:
ADR-0004 — One seeded RNG resource instead of scattered generators
Status: accepted
Context: Randomness (spread, crits, spawns) must reproduce exactly across runs, clients and platforms, and rewind cleanly in a rollback. A rand::thread_rng() anywhere in the simulation destroys all of that.
Decision: One seeded resource, SimRng (Xoshiro256** seeded via SplitMix64, own implementation, no external RNG crate), seeded from the scenario. It is the only randomness source in the simulation; clippy.toml forbids every other (RandomState, Instant::now, SystemTime::now).
Rejected alternative: rand with per-system SmallRngs. Convenient, but unseedable as a whole and impossible to rewind or audit.
Consequences: Same seed → same sequence everywhere; the RNG state is part of the snapshot for rollback; randomness consumption is auditable in one place. Costs: every draw must go through the resource; the draw order is part of the contract.

decisions/adr-0005-simulation-as-its-own.title: ADR-0005 — The simulation as its own crate
decisions/adr-0005-simulation-as-its-own.content:
ADR-0005 — The simulation as its own crate
Status: accepted
Context: The simulation must run without window, renderer, audio or threads — in tests, on a server, in RL training, and as wasm in the browser. In a single-crate game it is only a matter of time before a gameplay system touches a rendering type, and then none of those environments work anymore.
Decision: The simulation is its own workspace crate, game_sim, with dependencies limited to bevy (core, no rendering features), Avian physics queries and serde. It must build for wasm32-unknown-unknown. The client (game_client) depends on the simulation, never the other way around.
Rejected alternative: One crate with feature flags separating “sim” from “client”. Cheaper at first, but the boundary erodes and CI cannot enforce it.
Consequences: The boundary is enforced by the compiler and CI (cargo check -p game_sim --target wasm32-…). Costs: a workspace, and Bevy types that are presentation-only must be mirrored as plain data.

decisions/adr-0006-rollback-with-the-ser.title: ADR-0006 — Rollback netcode with the server as referee
decisions/adr-0006-rollback-with-the-ser.content:
ADR-0006 — Rollback netcode with the server as referee
Status: default (ADR-0012)
Context: PvP should feel instant even under latency. Lockstep stalls everyone on the slowest input; client-server with server simulation means the server, not the player, decides what happened — and costs hosting per tick.
Decision: Rollback netcode: every client simulates the whole game locally at full frame rate and predicts; when a late intent arrives, it rewinds to the last confirmed tick and re-simulates to the present. A server acts as referee: it validates intents, owns the authoritative tick, decides conflicts, and sends each client only the observation it is allowed to see. When they disagree, the server wins.
Rejected alternatives: Lockstep (stalls on the slowest player) and pure server simulation (input lag for everyone; server load per tick).
Consequences: Local input has zero latency; the deterministic simulation and serialisable intents (ADR-0001, ADR-0002) make the rewind exact. Costs: the simulation must be fast enough to re-run several ticks per frame; the server is a trusted component; desyncs need detection and handling.
Implemented so far: crates/game_sim/src/rollback.rs — a headless RollbackSession that keeps a window of snapshots and re-simulates when an intent arrives late; tested against the on-time run in tests/rollback.rs. No transport, no server yet.
To replace: for lockstep, client-server prediction or a single-player game, delete rollback.rs and tests/rollback.rs, supersede this ADR, and update Network. Snapshots, replays and the state hash stay: they serve save games and desync checks in every model.

decisions/adr-0007-observation-as-the-si.title: ADR-0007 — The observation as the single code path for reading state
decisions/adr-0007-observation-as-the-si.content:
ADR-0007 — The observation as the single code path for reading state
Status: accepted
Context: HUD, AI, add-ons and the network all need simulation state. If each reads the ECS world directly, visibility is enforced in many places (or nowhere), AI sees more than players, and the network leaks data.
Decision: One observation interface: a function that snapshots what a given team may see this tick, with a visibility filter. HUD, AI, add-ons and network sending read it and nothing else. It returns plain, serialisable data.
Rejected alternative: Direct Query access per consumer. More flexible, but visibility, versioning and auditing become impossible.
Consequences: Visibility has one place to be audited; AI trains on exactly what a player sees; the network sends exactly what the observation returns. Costs: one more layer, and the observation format must be versioned like the intent.

decisions/adr-0008-simid-instead-of-enti.title: ADR-0008 — SimId instead of entity index for ordering and serialisation
decisions/adr-0008-simid-instead-of-enti.content:
ADR-0008 — SimId instead of entity index for ordering and serialisation
Status: accepted
Context: Bevy Entity indices are ephemeral and unordered: the same scenario can assign different indices on different runs, and iteration order over archetypes is not a contract. Anything that orders gameplay, hashes on entities, or serialises them will desync.
Decision: Every simulated entity carries a stable SimId (i64, assigned in spawn order). All ordering, hashing and serialisation in the simulation keys on SimId, never on Entity.
Rejected alternative: Ordering by Entity. Free, but non-deterministic across runs and meaningless over the network.
Consequences: Deterministic ordering and stable wire formats; rollback snapshots reference entities that still mean the same thing after a rewind. Costs: one spawn counter to maintain and a lookup from ID to entity.

decisions/adr-0009-platform-neutrality.title: ADR-0009 — Platform neutrality: the simulation builds for wasm32
decisions/adr-0009-platform-neutrality.content:
ADR-0009 — Platform neutrality: the simulation builds for wasm32
Status: accepted
Context: Targets are Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS and, when feasible, the web. A dependency that pulls in threads, file system access or system time into the simulation excludes web — and usually breaks headless servers and RL training too.
Decision: game_sim must always build for wasm32-unknown-unknown: no threads, no file system, no system time, no clock. CI checks the wasm target (and Android, iOS) on every change. Every new dependency is checked for platform support before it enters Cargo.toml.
Rejected alternative: Deciding platforms per feature, late. Costs: rewrites, and features that cannot be undone once shipped.
Consequences: Web stays an option for free; the simulation stays embeddable everywhere. Costs: some convenient crates (threads, std::time, file logging) are off limits in the simulation; the client carries the platform-specific parts alone.

decisions/adr-0010-central-balance-resou.title: ADR-0010 — Central balance resource instead of magic numbers
decisions/adr-0010-central-balance-resou.content:
ADR-0010 — Central balance resource instead of magic numbers
Status: accepted
Context: Gameplay constants (speeds, damages, cooldowns) change constantly during balancing. Buried as magic numbers in systems, they are unfindable, untestable and undocumented — and later not exchangeable per game mode or by the server.
Decision: Every gameplay constant lives in the central Balance resource (one place, documented, typed). Systems read from it; magic numbers in systems are a review error. Later, balance variants become data.
Rejected alternative: Constants in the systems that use them. Local and obvious at first, but balancing becomes archaeology.
Consequences: Balancing happens in one file; constants can be serialised, diffed and shared with the server. Costs: one more parameter in almost every system signature.

decisions/adr-0011-rust-and-bevy.title: ADR-0011 — Rust with Bevy and Avian
decisions/adr-0011-rust-and-bevy.content:
ADR-0011 — Rust with Bevy and Avian
Status: accepted; the Avian part is a template default, see ADR-0015
Context: The architecture needs a game engine that runs gameplay headless in a fixed timestep, serialises state cheaply, builds for desktop, mobile and web, and stays debuggable down to the source. Proprietary engines fight the deterministic-simulation design; most others do not reach the platforms.
Decision: Rust with Bevy (ECS, app scheduling, rendering, assets) and Avian (physics queries; kinematic movement, shape casts). No gameplay logic in visual scripting; everything is Rust in this repository.
Rejected alternatives: Godot/Unity (determinism and headless testing fight the engine; licensing), raw Rust without an engine (renderer, input and asset pipelines would be rebuilt for years).
Consequences: One language for simulation and presentation; the ECS fits the intent/observation model perfectly; the whole toolchain is free and inspectable. Costs: Bevy moves fast — APIs change between versions and migrations are regular work; platform-specific edge cases are ours to solve.

decisions/adr-0012-template-defaults-dec.title: ADR-0012 — Genre-dependent decisions ship as template defaults, decided per game
decisions/adr-0012-template-defaults-dec.content:
ADR-0012 — Genre-dependent decisions ship as template defaults, decided per game
Status: accepted
Context: The template is used before anyone knows the genre: RPG, racing game, RTS, shooter, 2D or 3D. Some decisions hold for every genre (a deterministic tick simulation, intents, stable IDs, one RNG, snapshots). Others depend on the genre: how players connect, the tick rate and number type, the physics engine, the gameplay itself, how the client looks. Leaving those out makes the template untestable and the first session of every game start from nothing; fixing them as accepted makes the template quietly choose a genre.
Decision: A genre-dependent decision is recorded as an ADR with status default. It ships a basic, working, tested implementation, so the rest of the template can be built and tested against it, and a To replace section naming exactly the code and docs it owns. The first sessions of a new game decide every default: accept it (status becomes accepted), replace it (a new ADR supersedes it, the owned code is rewritten), or drop it (the owned code is deleted, the status becomes superseded). Nobody builds new code on a default without asking the maintainer. Defaults from this ADR on: ADR-0006 (rollback netcode), ADR-0013 (the example game), ADR-0014 (tick rate and number type), ADR-0015 (Avian; the rest of ADR-0011 stays accepted), ADR-0016 (the client shell), ADR-0017 (the save and replay file format).
Rejected alternatives: No genre code at all (nothing to test the core against; the client would show nothing), accepted decisions for one genre (the template would be a game, not a template), feature flags per genre (every combination would need testing and maintaining).
Consequences: The template runs, plays and is tested end to end, while a new game sees at a glance which decisions are still open. Costs: defaults are code that may be thrown away; the core must stay independent of them (the game module contract in crates/game_sim/src/game/mod.rs), or replacing one would ripple through everything.

decisions/adr-0013-example-game-units-on.title: ADR-0013 — The example game: units moving on an arena
decisions/adr-0013-example-game-units-on.content:
ADR-0013 — The example game: units moving on an arena
Status: default (ADR-0012)
Context: The genre-neutral core (ticks, intents, snapshots, replays, rollback, observation) needs real gameplay to be exercised: something that moves, uses randomness, and reaches a boundary, so the determinism tests can fail.
Decision: The template ships a minimal example: a few units spawned on a circle, moving on a disc-shaped arena floor (the x/z plane) by Move/Idle intents, with the stages Intent → Values → Movement → Damage → Cleanup inside SimSet::Update. The client draws it from above, one capsule per unit, and steers unit 1 with the move axis.
Rejected alternatives: A bare core with no gameplay (the determinism tests would pass trivially), a full sample game (more to delete, and it would bias every new game towards its genre).
Consequences: Everything in the template is tested against real gameplay; the game module shows what the core needs from a game. Costs: none beyond deleting it.
To replace: rewrite crates/game_sim/src/game/ keeping the contract in its mod.rs; rewrite crates/game_client/src/presentation.rs; replace the scripted runs in crates/game_sim/tests/determinism.rs and tests/regression.rs with ones that exercise the new systems, commit the new hash and re-record the regression replay; adapt tests/simulation.rs, tests/snapshot.rs, tests/replay.rs, tests/rollback.rs, tests/observation.rs to the new Setup and Action; update the tick chain in Simulation model.

decisions/adr-0014-sixty-ticks-per-secon.title: ADR-0014 — 60 ticks per second with f32 maths
decisions/adr-0014-sixty-ticks-per-secon.content:
ADR-0014 — 60 ticks per second with f32 maths
Status: default (ADR-0012)
Context: The tick rate and the number type depend on the genre. A shooter or fighting game wants 60 ticks per second or more; racing physics often 120 or more with substeps; a strategy game with thousands of units 10–20, and possibly fixed-point maths so every machine computes bit-identical results.
Decision: TICKS_PER_SECOND = 60 and f32 (Bevy’s Vec3), restricted to the operations IEEE 754 defines exactly (+ - * /, sqrt) in the simulation. CI compares a committed state hash on Linux, Windows and macOS (x86-64 and ARM64).
Rejected alternatives: Fixed-point from the start (slower to write, no Bevy maths types, and unnecessary for many genres), Bevy’s default of 64 Hz (no reason for it; 60 matches common displays).
Consequences: The example runs smoothly and its runs match bit for bit across the CI platforms. Costs: f32 determinism holds only as long as the simulation avoids platform maths functions (sin, cos, powf, …) and compiler settings stay the same; see Determinism.
To replace: change TICKS_PER_SECOND in crates/game_sim/src/lib.rs (and balance rates that assume 60); for fixed-point, replace Vec3/f32 in the game’s state, StateHasher::write_f32 users, and the observation, then commit the new determinism hash.

decisions/adr-0015-avian-for-physics.title: ADR-0015 — Avian for physics
decisions/adr-0015-avian-for-physics.content:
ADR-0015 — Avian for physics
Status: default (ADR-0012); splits the Avian part off ADR-0011, whose Rust-and-Bevy part stays accepted
Context: Whether a game needs physics, and which, depends on the genre: a racing game needs vehicle dynamics; a shooter needs ray and shape casts; an RTS or an RPG may need only simple collision checks, or none. Physics inside a deterministic simulation must run single-threaded and in a fixed order.
Decision: Avian (avian3d) is a dependency of game_sim, without its parallel and debug-plugin features, for collision and spatial queries. The example game does not use it yet.
Rejected alternatives: Rapier directly (Avian integrates with Bevy’s ECS and schedules), no physics dependency (every 3D game would start by choosing one; the wasm/mobile build checks would not cover it).
Consequences: The template proves Avian builds for every target in CI. Costs: compile time for a dependency the example does not use.
To replace: remove avian3d from the workspace and crates/game_sim/Cargo.toml (or switch to avian2d for a 2D game), run cargo clean once, and update Platforms.

decisions/adr-0016-client-shell.title: ADR-0016 — The client shell: screens, input actions, localisation, debug overlay
decisions/adr-0016-client-shell.content:
ADR-0016 — The client shell: screens, input actions, localisation, debug overlay
Status: default (ADR-0012)
Context: Every game needs a screen flow, device-independent input, translated texts and a way to see the simulation’s state while playing — and the rules forbid visible text and key bindings in code. Mature crates exist for each (Fluent for texts, input-manager crates for actions), but each is a dependency with its own release cycle against Bevy’s, and the right choice depends on the game’s size.
Decision: Small, dependency-free implementations in crates/game_client: screens (menu → playing ⇄ paused → menu, pausing virtual time pauses the simulation); a run setup (the scenario every run from the menu starts from, the local player and the viewer; the local actor is the unit the observation says that player controls); input actions (keyboard and gamepad equal, default bindings in data/input/bindings.txt with Bevy’s own key and button names, resolved by reflection); localisation (key = value files in data/locales/, compiled in, {name} placeholders, a missing key shows as itself); a UI font (Noto Sans Regular under the SIL OFL 1.1 in data/fonts/, compiled in and put in place of Bevy’s ASCII-only default font, so every text uses it; a test checks it has a glyph for every character of every locale); a debug overlay (tick, state hash, frame rate; toggle-debug action; the hash is computed only while the overlay is visible); save and load (save/load actions on one quicksave slot, a localised notice for every outcome including each reason a file is refused; loading from the menu starts the loaded run) over a storage of named byte slots with one backend per platform (files in the user’s data folder on desktop and iOS, found from the environment without a dependency; the app’s internal data folder on Android; localStorage with the bytes as base64 on the web).
Rejected alternatives: Fluent and an input-manager crate now (dependencies chosen before anyone knows what the game needs), nothing (every game would start by writing the same scaffolding, and the template’s client could not be played).
Consequences: The client is playable on keyboard and gamepad, and every text and binding is data. Costs: no plural rules or grammar in localisation, no rebinding UI, no saved settings yet, one save slot only; one font face (no bold or italic), covering Latin, Greek and Cyrillic only — scripts such as CJK, Arabic or Devanagari need another font (and complex shaping); Bevy’s own default font still ships in the binary.
To replace: each part is one module (screens.rs, run.rs, input.rs, localisation.rs with kv.rs, font.rs, overlay.rs, saving.rs, storage.rs) plus its data file; replace a module and keep its resource names (ActionState, Localisation, RunSetup), or change their users.

decisions/adr-0017-postcard-files-with-a.title: ADR-0017 — Save and replay files: postcard behind a versioned header
decisions/adr-0017-postcard-files-with-a.content:
ADR-0017 — Save and replay files: postcard behind a versioned header
Status: default (ADR-0012)
Context: Save games and replays must become bytes: to store them, to attach a replay to a bug report, to commit a regression replay that CI plays back. The encoding must build for every target (the simulation has no file system on wasm), reproduce f32 values bit for bit, and stay stable. A deterministic replay only reproduces its run on the simulation behaviour that recorded it, whatever the format, so old files must be recognised and refused rather than silently diverge.
Decision: postcard (no_std, stable wire format since 1.0, floats as raw bits) behind a header: magic GSIM, the container FORMAT_VERSION, the file kind (save or replay), and the game’s SIM_VERSION. game_sim::file encodes and decodes; loading refuses foreign bytes, other formats, the wrong kind, other simulation versions, and damaged or padded payloads, each with its own FileError. A save also stores its state hash and is refused if the state does not match it. Replays record intents as they arrived, before the checks, so playback runs validation and control again. The simulation only produces bytes; the client decides where they are stored. A regression replay (crates/game_sim/tests/data/regression.replay) is played back by CI on every platform.
Rejected alternatives: RON or JSON (readable and diffable, but 5–10× larger and slower; readability matters little for files that must be re-recorded on every behaviour change anyway), MessagePack/CBOR (self-describing, but a deterministic replay cannot survive schema changes by tolerance alone; bigger than postcard), bincode (a second major API in a short time; no specified wire format).
Consequences: Saves and replays are small (ten seconds of five players: about 1.2 KB) and identical on every platform; the same encoding can later carry intents over the network. Costs: the files are not human-readable (Debug printing is the way to inspect them); every behaviour change means bumping SIM_VERSION and re-recording the regression replay, which the failing test explains; old saves stop loading after such a bump, so a shipped game needs a migration path before it promises save compatibility.
To replace: change crates/game_sim/src/file.rs (and the postcard dependency in both Cargo.tomls), bump FORMAT_VERSION, re-record the regression replay. save.rs and replay.rs only call file::encode/file::decode.

glossary.title: Glossary — terms from intent to rollback
glossary.content:
Glossary — terms from intent to rollback

































































































TermMeaningTickOne step of the simulation, 1 / TICKS_PER_SECOND seconds. All durations in the simulation are ticks.IntentPlain, serialisable data saying what a unit wants to do in a tick. The only thing the presentation writes back.SimulationThe deterministic gameplay in game_sim, running in FixedUpdate, headless-capable.PresentationEverything the player sees: rendering, HUD, animation, sound. A pure observer.ObservationThe one function through which HUD, AI, add-ons and the network read simulation state, filtered by visibility.SimIdA stable ID for simulation entities; ordering and serialisation key on it, never on Entity.SimRngThe one seeded RNG resource; the only randomness source in the simulation.ScenarioThe complete start state of a run: the seed and the game’s Setup. Same scenario + same inputs = same end state.SnapshotThe whole simulation state as one value (tick, RNG, ID counter, control, game state); restoring it and re-running the same intents gives the same state.PlayerWhoever sends intents: a person, an AI or an add-on, numbered by PlayerId.ControlWhich player may steer which actor; intents from anyone else are rejected.State hashA platform-independent checksum of a snapshot; equal states hash equally. Compared by determinism tests, replays and desync checks.ReplayA scenario plus the intents that arrived in every tick, and the final state hash playback must reach. Stored as a file (ADR-0017).Save gameA scenario, a snapshot and its state hash: continues a run exactly.SIM_VERSIONThe version of the simulation’s behaviour, recorded in every file. Bumped whenever a change alters what a run produces; files from other versions are refused.Template defaultAn ADR with status default: a genre-dependent decision the template ships working code for, decided per game (ADR-0012).RollbackNetcode technique: a client predicts ahead and rewinds to a confirmed state when a late input arrives.RefereeThe server that decides in conflicts; each client only computes what it is allowed to see.ADRArchitecture Decision Record: one decision, its context, the rejected alternative, its consequences.PAn open problem page: a question, who is affected, and its next step.VaultThis documentation: an Obsidian-style folder of linked Markdown pages, published as a website.BalanceThe central resource holding all gameplay constants; no magic numbers in systems.

index.title: Game Template
index.content:
Game Template
Game Template is the starting point for every new game of Magier SpieleSchmiede: a game in Rust with Bevy, whose entire gameplay is a deterministic, headless tick simulation in its own crate; the presentation is a pure observer that writes back exactly one thing, the intent. Randomness comes from the one seeded RNG resource; all durations are ticks. Planned for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS, with keyboard/mouse and gamepad alike. Genre-dependent choices — how players connect, tick rate, physics, the gameplay itself, the client’s look — ship as template defaults: working code a new game accepts, replaces or drops (Decisions). Later come PvP, AI opponents, add-ons and more — designed for, not built yet. This vault documents the template: specification, architecture, decisions, test strategy and open problems, one page per topic.

milestones/extension-points.content:

testing/benchmarks.content:
Benchmarks — performance before and after
Whoever changes the simulation or rendering compares before and after:

Simulation: ticks per second of the headless app with a representative scenario (units, abilities, projectiles). Rollback needs headroom — the sim must re-run several ticks per frame.
Rendering: frame time of the client on the minimum hardware (see the problem log for the budget question).

Rules:

Measure on the same machine, same power mode, nothing else running; report median and spread, not a single run.
A regression that exceeds the budget blocks the change until explained or fixed.
Benchmarks are scripts in the repository, so “before” is reproducible from the previous commit.

The headless benchmark
cargo run -p game_sim --release --example bench
cargo run -p game_sim --release --example bench -- --units 2,100,1000 --ticks 600 --runs 7 --window 8
crates/game_sim/examples/bench.rs prints a Markdown table, one row per scenario size. Every unit gets a move intent every tick. Each figure is the median over the runs, with min–max beside it. Afterwards run cargo clean --release (AGENTS.md).

Results
2026-11-17, template example game, SIM_VERSION 1. Cloud container, 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz), shared, so the spread is wide. Release build, 600 ticks, 7 runs, window 8; µs, median (min–max):

Reading them:

About 8 µs per tick is fixed cost of Bevy’s schedules with almost nothing to do; above that, cost grows roughly linearly with units (about 0.11 µs per unit and tick).
Restore costs about six captures, since it despawns and respawns every simulation entity.
The state hash costs about 66 ns per unit, almost four times a capture. The client computes it once per tick only while the debug overlay is visible (T-014); desync checks would run it per tick, so it is the first thing to look at if large scenarios matter.
Even at 1000 units, an 8-tick rollback takes about 1.1 ms of a 16.7 ms frame: the example game leaves rollback plenty of headroom. A real game re-measures with its own systems.

testing/determinism-test.title: Determinism test — same scenario, same end state
testing/determinism-test.content:
Determinism test — same scenario, same end state
The contract of the whole architecture, as an executable check (crates/game_sim/tests/determinism.rs):

Build two headless apps from the same scenario (same seed, same units).
Feed identical scripted intents into both — moves in several directions, long enough to reach the arena edge.
Step both the same number of ticks.
Assert, in SimId order: every unit’s position, velocity and health are exactly equal, and so is the state_hash (which includes the RNG state).
Assert that the moving units did move: two runs in which nothing happens agree trivially.

Two more tests guard against trivial passes and against platform drift:

Different seeds diverge.
Committed hash: the scripted run’s state_hash (crates/game_sim/src/checksum.rs) must equal a value committed in the test. CI runs it on Linux, Windows and macOS, so it checks the same run across platforms, not only within one process. A deliberate change to the simulation that changes the value updates it in the same commit, saying why.

Rules:

The test must stay green under every change to the simulation; a red determinism test blocks the commit, no exceptions.
Extend it as the state grows: every field that desyncs PvP belongs in the comparison.
Extend state_hash as the state grows, in the same way.
The regression replay (crates/game_sim/tests/regression.rs) is the same idea as a file: a recorded run in tests/data/regression.replay, played back on every CI platform. It also covers the file format and the intent checks (the run contains rejected intents). On a deliberate behaviour change, bump game::SIM_VERSION and re-record: cargo test -p game_sim --test regression -- --ignored record_regression_replay.
The committed hash covers the desktop CI runners only (x86-64 and ARM64 macOS); mobile and wasm are only built, not run. Full cross-platform floating-point determinism stays an open question (see the Problem log).

testing/headless-integration-test.title: Headless integration test — the simulation without a window
testing/headless-integration-test.content:
Headless integration test — the simulation without a window
The normal case for tests, benchmarks, the server and RL training is the headless app (game_sim::headless):
let mut app = headless_app(Scenario { seed: 42, setup: Setup { unit_count: 2 } });
step_ticks(&mut app, 600); // ten simulated seconds
What it guarantees:

No window, no renderer, no threads: time never comes from a clock; every App::update advances exactly one fixed timestep, so FixedUpdate runs exactly once.
Startup runs once, before the app is handed out, so the first step_ticks is already a real tick.
A test that needs no randomness beyond the scenario needs no setup at all.

Rules: integration tests live in crates/game_sim/tests/; they script intents, step ticks and assert on simulation state (the game’s components, the observation, or the state hash); they never read presentation state.

testing/test-strategy.content:
Test strategy — what is tested how, and where the boundaries are

Principles:

Tests first: the failing test pins the behaviour before the implementation.
The simulation is tested headless; nothing gameplay needs a window.
The presentation’s logic (bindings, localisation, interpolation, save and load) is unit-tested; the rendering itself is exercised by playing and by platform CI.
Every test that touches randomness seeds its SimRng; every test that touches time counts ticks.

The gates before every commit: cargo fmt --check, cargo check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test.
